sections.body:
Psychological manipulation is the use of pressure, ambiguity or emotion to move a person into a decision that does not serve them. The person is shown a choice, and the choice is built so that it feels like the only one. The point is not to win an argument. It is to produce a decision that the person believes was theirs.

Persuasion is different, and the difference is easy to state. Persuasion gives you a real choice and expects you to use it. A good salesperson explains the product, names the price and lets you say no. **Pressure** sits between the two: a deadline, a discount that ends tonight, a manager who wants an answer now. Pressure on its own is ordinary. Pressure becomes manipulation when the push is arranged so that saying no is difficult, humiliating or costly.

Coercion is stronger again. Coercion takes the choice away by force or by the threat of harm — to your job, your money, your safety, or the safety of somebody close to you. Coercion leaves evidence, because it usually needs a threat. Manipulation is harder to prove, because it works on the mind, where nothing is left behind.

So the four words sit on one line. Persuasion leaves the choice open. Pressure narrows it. Coercion removes it. Manipulation works on you until you believe the choice was never there.
examples: This is persuasion: I can say no, and the offer will still be there tomorrow.
That was pressure. Pressure stops being ordinary when saying no becomes difficult.
Sign today or lose your job — that is coercion, not persuasion.
sections.heading: What manipulation is, and how it differs from persuasion

terms.example: It was manipulation: he offered her two options and made the wrong one impossible.
terms.gloss: The use of pressure, ambiguity or emotion to move a person into a decision that does not serve them, without giving a real choice.

terms.example: That was persuasion, not pressure: he explained the plan and left the decision to her.
terms.gloss: An honest attempt to win agreement, in which the other person is free to say no.

terms.example: The deadline is pressure, but you can still say that you need more time.
terms.gloss: A push applied to a decision, usually through time or emotion, that makes the choice harder to refuse.

terms.example: Sign the form today or lose the job — that is coercion, not persuasion.
terms.gloss: The removal of a real choice by force or by the threat of harm.

sections.body:
The fast patterns arrive inside one conversation, and each one has a fixed set of words. Once you know them, you can hear them in a sentence. **Social proof** is the claim that other people have already decided: *"Everyone is buying this one"*, *"Half the team has already signed up"*, *"It is the most popular model this month"*. Social proof is not a lie by itself. It becomes a pressure tactic when the people it names are invented, or when the crowd it describes has nothing to do with your situation.

Authority is the claim that the speaker knows better than you: *"The specialist says this is the only safe option"*, *"I have worked with this machine for twenty years"*, *"Trust me, I know this system"*. Authority is honest when the knowledge is real and the evidence is shown. It is manipulation when the title is used in place of the evidence. **Scarcity** limits the supply: *"Only two left"*, *"The price goes up at midnight"*, *"This price ends today"*. Scarcity is the easiest of the five to check, because it can be counted. Ask how many are left, and ask who is counting them.

Urgency shortens the time you have to think: *"Decide now"*, *"I need an answer before I close the order"*, *"The offer is off the table at five"*. **Fear** raises the price of thinking slowly: *"If you do not sign now, you lose the deposit"*, *"If you do not back up the machine tonight, you lose the whole line"*. Urgency and fear are often used together: one removes the time to check, and the other makes the delay feel dangerous.

None of these five needs a villain. A tired supervisor, a salesman on a target, a colleague who wants to help you, a friend who is excited — any of them can use these words without meaning any harm. The question is not whether the person is bad. The question is whether the words are doing the deciding for you. If you cannot repeat the conditions in your own words — the price, the deadline, what happens if you say no — you are hearing a pattern, not a decision.
examples: How many are left? If the number is small, the price should not change tomorrow.
Let me check that in the manual before I answer.
I am not saying no. I am asking for the answer in writing.
sections.heading: The fast patterns: social proof, authority, scarcity, urgency and fear

terms.example: The offer came with social proof: nine out of ten customers chose the larger plan.
terms.gloss: A pressure tactic that presents the decisions of other people as evidence for your own.

terms.example: It used authority: the technician said the part was safe, and showed no manual.
terms.gloss: A pressure tactic that puts the decision in the hands of an expert, real or claimed.

terms.example: The scarcity was easy to check: the shelf held six, not two.
terms.gloss: A pressure tactic that claims the supply is limited, so that waiting looks like a loss.

terms.example: The urgency was built to stop a phone call: sign tonight or the price changes.
terms.gloss: A pressure tactic that shortens the time available for checking and deciding.

terms.example: The fear in the message was plain: if you wait, you are the one who pays.
terms.gloss: A pressure tactic that raises the cost of a slow decision, so that speed feels like safety.

sections.body:
The fast patterns, plus three slow ones, are enough to read most situations that are being pushed. The middle column is the useful one. It gives you the words, and the words are what you will actually hear on the day.

Read the table once and keep it. In the middle of a conversation you will not remember the definitions, but you will remember the sentence *"Only two left"* or *"Everyone has already signed"*. That is enough to know that a decision is being made for you.
examples: Only two left — so how many are there, and who counts them?
Please send me the terms in writing.
I want the price in an email I can read later.
sections.heading: The pattern, the words, and what it does to the decision

headers: What it does to the decision
rows: Social proof
"Everyone is buying this one." "Half the team has already signed up."
Puts the decision in the hands of a crowd, so a number settles it instead of you.
Authority
"The specialist says this is the only safe option." "Trust me, I know this machine."
Moves the decision to somebody else's judgement, and you stop checking the facts.
False scarcity
"Only two left." "The price goes up at midnight."
Makes waiting look like a loss, so you buy to keep an option rather than because the option is good.
Urgency
"I need an answer before I close the order." "This ends tonight."
Removes the time you need to check, and the check is the only protection there is.
Fear
"If you do not sign now, you lose the deposit."
Turns a slow decision into a risk you cannot carry, so you act to make the fear stop.
The sunk cost
"You have already paid for the training." "The rest of the year is nearly done."
Makes you protect what you have spent instead of asking whether the next part is worth it.
Love bombing
"I have never met anyone like you." "You are the only one I trust."
Floods the decision with feeling, so a warning sign reads as warmth.
Gaslighting
"That is not what you said." "You are forgetting things again."
Turns your check on the outside world into a doubt about your own memory.

terms.example: The sunk cost of the training was the argument for staying in the job.
terms.gloss: Money, time or effort that has already been spent, and which is used as a reason to continue.

terms.example: The love bombing was hard to refuse: every message came with a declaration.
terms.gloss: Attention, affection and gifts given far faster and further than the situation deserves.

terms.example: It was gaslighting: she was told her own account of the meeting was wrong.
terms.gloss: A repeated attack on a person's memory and judgement, so that they stop trusting what they remember.

sections.body:
The slow patterns do not work in one conversation. They work over days or months, and each one starts small. You cannot spot them by listening for a key phrase, because the phrase is not the pattern. The pattern is in the direction. **The foot in the door** is the smallest of them: you agree to something small and easy — a free trial, a short meeting, a signature on a form — and that small agreement becomes the reason for the next, larger one: *"You have already started, so it would be a waste to stop now"*. The small yes was never really about the small thing.

The sunk cost is the same idea turned on the past. What you have already paid, spent or learned is treated as a reason to continue, and the question of what to do *now* is never asked. The words are *"You have already paid for the training"* and *"The rest of the year is nearly done"*. What is already spent cannot be saved by spending more. **Love bombing** works the other way round: attention is given far faster and further than the situation deserves — messages all night, gifts early, declarations in the first week, and remarks like *"I have never met anyone like you"*. It feels like being understood, and it makes every later warning invisible.

Gaslighting is a steady attack on your memory and your judgement, dressed as disagreement. The statements are small and repeated: *"That is not what you said"*, *"You are forgetting things again"*, *"Nobody would believe you"*. The aim is not to win an argument. It is to make you stop trusting what you remember, so that somebody else has to tell you what is true.

Isolation is the slowest of all. The people who would say no to you are removed one by one from the picture: *"You do not need to bring her"*, *"Your family would not understand this"*, *"Keep this between us"*. Each removal looks like a private preference. Together they leave one person with nobody to check with.
examples: You have already started, so it would be a waste to stop now — and that is the whole trick.
Keep this between us? Then I will take my time.
I remember what was said, and I have written it down.
sections.heading: The slow patterns: a small yes, the sunk cost, love bombing, gaslighting and isolation

terms.example: The free trial was the foot in the door: the yearly contract came next.
terms.gloss: A small, easy agreement that is used later as the reason for a much larger one.

terms.example: The isolation was quiet: her friends stopped being invited, one by one.
terms.gloss: The slow removal of the people who would tell a person the truth, one person at a time.

sections.body:
The words in this section are the ones used in workplace policy, in health care, in the law and in the reports written after something has gone wrong. They are worth learning for two reasons: you can name what is happening, and you can use the name in writing.

Undue influence is the phrase used in law and in medical consent for pressure strong enough to take away somebody's freedom to decide. **A pressure tactic** is one move made to push a decision: a deadline, a discount, a display of authority, a comparison with other people. **Consent** is the agreement itself, and it only counts when it is free, informed, and given by a person who can still say no. **A boundary** is the line you draw in advance: what you will do, what you will not do, and what you need before you answer. **Coercive control** is the name for a pattern in which one person keeps control by limiting another person's money, their time or their contact with other people, and by making it costly to refuse.

Manipulation, **coercion** and **gaslighting** belong to the same set, and they are the three words most likely to be heard. Manipulation is the umbrella word. Coercion is its hard edge, because a threat is involved. Gaslighting is the slow form, because it works on memory over weeks. If you write a report, use the word that fits what actually happened, and not the one that sounds worst.
examples: In writing: I want to read the terms before I agree to anything.
That is not consent if I cannot change my mind.
My boundary is simple: I do not sign anything at the counter.
sections.heading: The words of the field

terms.example: The form said the signature was voluntary; the manager's tone made that undue influence.
terms.gloss: Pressure strong enough to take away a person's freedom to decide, in the sense used in law and in medical consent.

terms.example: The second call was a pressure tactic: it moved the deadline by one hour.
terms.gloss: One move made to push a decision, such as a deadline, a discount or a display of authority.

terms.example: Without consent the order is not a contract, whatever the form says.
terms.gloss: Agreement that is free, informed, and given by a person who is still able to say no.

terms.example: My boundary is simple: I do not sign anything at the counter.
terms.gloss: The line you draw in advance: what you will do, what you will not do, and what you need before you answer.

terms.example: The pattern of coercive control is recognised by what it restricts, not by what it says.
terms.gloss: A pattern in which one person keeps control over another by limiting their money, their time or their contact with other people.

sections.body:
The steps below work on any situation: a purchase, a contract, a request at work, a conversation with somebody you trust less than they would like. The order matters. The first step does most of the work, and the last step makes the next time easier.

Two rules run through all six steps. You are not accusing anybody: you are buying time, asking for information, and keeping a record. And every step fits into one sentence — the sentences are at the end of this article.
examples: I need to think about this and come back to you tomorrow.
Please send the price and the deadline in writing.
Let me check that with someone before I answer.
sections.heading: How to step out of it
steps: Slow the moment down. Move the decision away from the moment it is being made: "I need to think about this, and I will answer tomorrow."
Ask for the offer in writing. The price, the scope, the deadline, and what happens if you say no: "Please send me the details in writing, so I can check them."
Check the facts with a source you chose yourself. A number in the contract, a call to the supplier, the manual, the colleague who is not part of the conversation.
Name the feeling you have: "I am flattered, and I am also uncomfortable, and I want to understand why." A named feeling is harder to argue with than a decision.
Check with somebody outside the situation: one person who is not part of it, who knows your situation, and who will tell you the truth.
Keep a short record. The date, the time, what was said, who said it, and what you answered. A note written the same day is worth more than a memory a month later.

sections.body:
This article names the patterns so that you can recognise them in your own life and in your work. It is not a manual. The words it lists belong to people who want a decision they cannot get honestly, and they are never to be used on another person.

If you notice yourself counting somebody's sentences, or checking the price of a decision for another person, stop. Naming a pattern is a way of protecting yourself. It is not a way of winning.
examples: The purpose of these words is to recognise them, not to use them.
Naming the pattern is how I protect myself, not how I win an argument.
sections.heading: This article is for defending yourself

sections.body:
These sentences are short, neutral and hard to argue with. None of them accuses anybody, and none of them gives up the decision. Use them in the same tone as the conversation around them. The flatness is the point.

The first three are for the moment itself. The rest are for what you write down afterwards.
examples: Take the time you need to decide.
Please send that in writing.
That is not a yes.
I want to see the terms before I agree to anything.
I am not comfortable with this, and I want to understand why.
Let me check that with someone before I answer.
I am not saying no. I am saying I will answer on Friday.
This is what was said, and this is when it was said.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

item.summary: Manipulation is not an argument you can win. It is pressure, ambiguity or emotion arranged so that a decision looks like it was yours. After reading this you can name the common patterns, tell persuasion apart from pressure and coercion, recognise the signs in yourself, and use six steps and a set of ready sentences to slow the moment down and keep a real choice.
item.title: Psychological Manipulation: How to Recognise It and Step Out
